```{r setup}
library(fgls)
```

## The problem

In \(y_t = x_t'\beta + u_t\) with autocorrelated errors, GLS (or its
feasible version) is more efficient than OLS. The classic feasible version,
Cochrane-Orcutt, estimates the error autocorrelation from OLS residuals. That
is fine when the regressors are *exogenous*, uncorrelated with the errors at all
leads and lags. Many time-series regressors are only *pre-determined*: they are
uncorrelated with current and future innovations, but respond to past ones, as
with policy variables, expectations and lagged prices. OLS is then inconsistent,
and so is Cochrane-Orcutt, which inherits its residuals.

## The estimator

The errors are approximated by an AR(k) process,
\(u_t = \rho_1 u_{t-1} + \dots + \rho_k u_{t-k} + e_t\).
Substituting \(u_t = y_t - x_t'\beta\) gives the **Durbin regression**

$$y_t = \sum_{j=1}^k \rho_j y_{t-j} + x_t'\beta - \sum_{j=1}^k x_{t-j}'\delta_j + e_t ,$$

estimated by OLS. Every regressor of this equation is uncorrelated with the
innovation \(e_t\) when \(x_t\) is pre-determined, so the coefficients on the
lagged \(y\) estimate the \(\rho_j\) consistently. In `fgls`:

1. the order \(k\) minimizes BIC over \(0, \dots, k_{max}\), all orders being
   fitted on the same sample (eq. 14);
2. the data are quasi-differenced with the estimated filter, every column
   including the constant, and the first \(k\) observations are dropped; OLS on
   the filtered data gives \(\hat\beta\) (eq. 15).

Lagged columns that duplicate other regressors (lags of the constant, of a
linear trend, of periodic dummies) are dropped automatically from the Durbin
regression.

## Table 1 of the paper

```{r table1}
sim <- simulate_serial(500, seed = 7) # AR(1) 0.8, x_t = v_t + e_{t-1}
fits <- list(
  OLS = ols_robust(y ~ x, data = sim),
  `Cochrane-Orcutt` = cochrane_orcutt(y ~ x, data = sim),
  Durbin = durbin_estimator(y ~ x, data = sim),
  FGLS = serial_fgls(y ~ x, data = sim),
  `GLS (known rho)` = infeasible_gls(y ~ x, data = sim, rho = 0.8)
)
sapply(fits, function(f) coef(f)[["x"]])
```

The true slope is 1. In the paper's Monte Carlo (10,000 replications) OLS has a
bias of about 0.40, Cochrane-Orcutt about 0.03, and FGLS is as precise as the
infeasible GLS; `vignette("validation")` reproduces these numbers with this
package.

## Variance and inference

Because \(\hat\rho\) is estimated, and the regressors may react to past
innovations, the usual GLS variance (`vcov = "naive"`, eq. 27) understates the
uncertainty of \(\hat\beta\). The default `vcov = "robust"` (eqs. 28--29) adds a
correction built from the covariance between the filtered regressors and past
residuals. It is valid whether the regressors are exogenous or merely
pre-determined, and it is positive semidefinite by construction.

```{r variance}
fit <- fits$FGLS
cbind(robust = sqrt(diag(vcov(fit))), naive = sqrt(diag(vcov(fit, type = "naive"))))
fit$nonexogeneity_share
```

`nonexogeneity_share` averages the relative increase of the robust over the
naive variance across coefficients. Values near zero mean the regressors
behave as exogenous.

## Lag selection

```{r ic}
plot(fit, which = 3)
fit$bic_path
```

`kmax` defaults to \(\lfloor 12 (T/200)^{1/4} \rfloor\) (12 at \(T = 200\), as in
the paper's simulations) and is capped so that the Durbin regression uses at
most half of the sample. `ar_order` fixes the order; `ic = "aic"` and
`fgls_control(min_lags = "adjusted")` are alternatives. With several stochastic
regressors, `fgls_control(ic_penalty = "params")` penalizes every coefficient a
lag adds.

## Lagged dependent variables

When lags of \(y\) are regressors, the Durbin coefficients on lagged \(y\) mix
the dynamics of the model with those of the errors. Under the common-factor
structure the AR coefficients can be recovered from the ratio of a lagged
regressor's coefficient to its contemporaneous one (Wallis, 1967; Section 4.2 of
the paper). Declare the lagged dependent variables:

```{r wallis}
set.seed(3)
n <- 400
w <- rnorm(n + 1)
u <- as.numeric(stats::filter(rnorm(n + 1), 0.5, method = "recursive"))
yy <- numeric(n + 1)
for (t in 2:(n + 1)) yy[t] <- 0.4 * yy[t - 1] + 1 + w[t] + u[t]
dyn <- data.frame(y = yy[-1], ylag = yy[-(n + 1)], w = w[-1])
fit_dyn <- serial_fgls(y ~ ylag + w, data = dyn, lagged_dep_vars = "ylag")
coef(fit_dyn)
fit_dyn$rho
```

Without the declaration, `fgls()` warns that a regressor looks like a lagged
dependent variable.

## MA(1) errors

For errors known to be MA(1), such as two-step-ahead forecast errors, the GMA
estimator (Section 5) inverts the MA filter with the maximum-likelihood
estimate of \(\theta\):

```{r gma}
pred <- simulate_predictive(300, theta = -0.4, seed = 4)
serial_fgls(y ~ x, data = pred, serial = "ma1")
```

## Checking pre-determinedness

`test_predetermined()` (experimental) is a variable-addition LM test for missing
lags of the regressors (Remark 9 of the paper). A rejection suggests adding lags
of the regressors to the model:

```{r predetermined}
suppressWarnings(test_predetermined(y ~ x, data = sim))
```
